claim: Multi-Region Access Points, based on AWS Global Accelerator, route requests over the AWS network to the lowest-latency replicated copy and improve performance by up to 60%.
question: What is an S3 Multi-Region Access Point?

evidence.quote: Amazon S3 Multi-Region Access Points accelerate performance by up to 60% when accessing data sets that are replicated across multiple AWS Regions. Based on AWS Global Accelerator, S3 Multi-Region Access Points consider factors like network congestion and the location of the requesting application to dynamically route your requests over the AWS network to the lowest latency copy of your data.

claim: A Multi-Region Access Point routes across one bucket per Region in up to 17 Regions, and S3 generates a single DNS-compatible name used as the global endpoint.
question: How many Regions can one Multi-Region Access Point span?

evidence.quote: You can configure your Multi-Region Access Point to route across one bucket per AWS Region, in up to 17 AWS Regions. When you create a Multi-Region Access Point, S3 automatically generates a DNS-compatible name. This name is used as a global endpoint that can be used by your clients.

claim: Multi-Region Access Points run active-active or active-passive; in active-passive, failover controls shift S3 request traffic to the alternate Region and account within minutes.
question: How do Multi-Region Access Point failover controls work?

evidence.quote: To directly control this routing, you can operate S3 Multi-Region Access Points in an active-active or active-passive configuration. In an active-passive configuration, you can use S3 Multi-Region Access Points failover controls to initiate a failover to shift S3 data access request traffic to the chosen alternate AWS Region and account within minutes.

claim: CRR moves data across Regions to create isolated replicas, while Multi-Region Access Points route requests across Regions; together they give a replicated multi-Region dataset behind a single global endpoint.
question: What is the difference between CRR and Multi-Region Access Points?

evidence.quote: S3 Multi-Region Access Points help you to manage requests across AWS Regions, while CRR allows you to move data across AWS Regions to create isolated replicas. You use S3 Multi-Region Access Points and CRR together to create a replicated multi-Region dataset that is addressable by a single global endpoint.

claim: The underlying buckets of a Multi-Region Access Point can be Requester Pays buckets; the requester then pays the request and data transfer cost of both the bucket and the access point.
question: Does Requester Pays work with Multi-Region Access Points?

evidence.quote: Yes, you can configure the underlying buckets of the S3 Multi-Region Access Point to be Requester Pays buckets. With Requester Pays, the requester pays all of the cost associated to the endpoint usage, including the cost for requests and data transfer cost associated with both the bucket and the Multi-Region Access Point.

claim: In general bucket owners pay for all S3 storage of their bucket; Requester Pays is for sharing data without paying for other people's access.
question: What does the bucket owner still pay with Requester Pays?

values.display: bucket owners pay for all Amazon S3 storage

evidence.quote: Typically, you want to configure your buckets as Requester Pays buckets if you wish to share data but not incur charges associated with others accessing the data. In general, bucket owners pay for all Amazon S3 storage associated with their bucket.

claim: By default replication copies metadata from the source objects to the replicas only; with replica modification sync, metadata changes made on replicas are replicated back to the source, making replication two-way.
question: What does replica modification sync do?

evidence.quote: By default, Amazon S3 replicates metadata from the source objects to the replicas only. When replica modification sync is enabled, Amazon S3 replicates metadata changes made to the replica copies back to the source object, making the replication bidirectional (two-way replication).

claim: Two-way replication is two rules: one from the source bucket to the bucket holding the replicas, and a second from that bucket back to the source; the buckets can be in the same or different Regions.
question: How do you set up two-way replication between two S3 buckets?

evidence.quote: To set up two-way replication, create a replication rule from the source bucket (`{{amzn-s3-demo-source-bucket}}`) to the bucket containing the replicas (`{{amzn-s3-demo-destination-bucket}}`). Then, create a second replication rule from the bucket containing the replicas (`{{amzn-s3-demo-destination-bucket}}`) to the source bucket (`{{amzn-s3-demo-source-bucket}}`). The source and destination buckets can be in the same or different AWS Regions.

claim: You must enable replica modification sync on both the source and destination buckets to replicate replica metadata changes such as ACLs, tags or Object Lock settings.
question: Where must replica modification sync be enabled?

values.display: on both the source and destination buckets

evidence.quote: You must enable replica modification sync on both the source and destination buckets to replicate replica metadata changes like object access control lists (ACLs), object tags, object annotations, or Object Lock settings on the replicated objects.

claim: Each S3 storage class charges a fee to store data and fees to access it; choose by access pattern and retention time for the lowest total cost over the data's lifetime.
question: What does AWS say to consider when choosing a storage class?

evidence.quote: Each S3 storage class charges a fee to store data and fees to access data. In deciding which S3 storage class best fits your workload, consider the access patterns and retention time of your data to optimize for the lowest total cost over the lifetime of your data.

claim: Choose S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval for archives that need immediate (milliseconds) access, S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval for retrieval in minutes or free bulk retrievals in 5-12 hours, and S3 Glacier Deep Archive, the lowest cost, for retrieval within 12 hours.
question: How do the three S3 Glacier classes differ?

evidence.quote: For archive data that does not require immediate access but needs the flexibility to retrieve large sets of data at no cost, such as backup or disaster recovery use cases, choose S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, with retrieval in minutes or free bulk retrievals in 5—12 hours. To save even more on long-lived archive storage such as compliance archives and digital media preservation, choose S3 Glacier Deep Archive, the lowest cost storage in the cloud with data retrieval within 12 hours.

claim: All S3 Glacier storage classes keep data on multiple devices across physically separated Availability Zones within a Region.
question: Are the S3 Glacier classes multi-AZ?

evidence.quote: All these storage classes provide multi-Availability Zone (AZ) resiliency by redundantly storing data on multiple devices and physically separated AWS Availability Zones in an AWS Region.

claim: S3 Express One Zone stores objects in a single Availability Zone, so it is a One Zone class; directory buckets are its only bucket type.
question: How many Availability Zones hold an S3 Express One Zone object?

evidence.quote: S3 directory buckets only allow objects stored in the S3 Express One Zone storage class, which provides faster data processing within a single Availability Zone.

claim: S3 Glacier Deep Archive works with object tagging, Lifecycle, Object Lock and Replication, and one bucket can mix Deep Archive with S3 Standard, Standard-IA, One Zone-IA and Flexible Retrieval objects.
question: Can one bucket hold Deep Archive objects next to S3 Standard objects?

values.display: a single Amazon S3 bucket to store a mixture

evidence.quote: S3 Glacier Deep Archive is integrated with Amazon S3 features, including S3 Object Tagging, S3 Lifecycle policies, S3 Object Lock, and S3 Replication. With S3 storage management features, you can use a single Amazon S3 bucket to store a mixture of S3 Glacier Deep Archive, S3 Standard, S3 Standard-IA, S3 One Zone-IA, and S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval data.

claim: Tape Gateway can archive virtual tapes directly to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive without changing existing backup workflows.
question: How do tape backups reach S3 Glacier Deep Archive?

values.display: Tape Gateway supports archiving your new virtual tapes directly

evidence.quote: With this feature, Tape Gateway supports archiving your new virtual tapes directly to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive, helping you meet your backup, archive, and recovery requirements. Tape Gateway helps you move tape-based backups to AWS without making any changes to your existing backup workflows.

claim: S3 Lifecycle can transition objects by age from S3 Standard to Standard-IA, One Zone-IA or the Glacier classes, expire objects by age, and expire incomplete multipart uploads by upload age.
question: What three kinds of action can an S3 Lifecycle policy take?

evidence.quote: You can also set lifecycle expiration policies to automatically remove objects based on the age of the object. You can set a policy for multipart upload expiration, which expires incomplete multipart uploads based on the age of the upload.
